Today most flashlights use LEDs, which are much brighter and last far longer than old bulbs. In Britain and many other countries the same tool is called a torch. A good flashlight is one of the simplest and most useful things to keep in an emergency kit.
ways: Check every flashlight and swap old batteries.
Build a small emergency kit for your home.
Make shadow puppets with kids tonight.

12-22|National Date Nut Bread Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Date Nut Bread Day. Date nut bread is a quick bread, meaning it rises with baking soda or baking powder instead of yeast. Chopped dates are often soaked in boiling water first so they soften and melt into the batter, and walnuts add crunch.

In the United States it became a classic holiday bread in the twentieth century, sometimes even sold in cans, and it is often served in slices with cream cheese. Dates bring natural sweetness and moisture, which is why the loaf stays soft for days.
ways: Bake a loaf of date nut bread.
Spread a slice with cream cheese.
Wrap a loaf as a neighbor gift.

12-22|Forefathers Day.story:
Forefathers Day remembers the Pilgrims' landing at Plymouth in 1620. The Old Colony Club in Plymouth first celebrated it in 1769, and the day is still marked in Plymouth with a procession and a traditional dinner that features succotash.

The date itself has a curious twist. The Pilgrims recorded the landing under the old calendar, and when converting to the modern calendar, the early celebrants added the wrong number of days. As a result, December 22 is used, though many historians place the landing on December 21.
ways: Read a short history of Plymouth Colony.
Cook a pot of succotash for dinner.
Look up your family's history online.

12-23|National Pfeffernusse Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Pfeffernusse Day. Pfeffernüsse are small, round spice cookies baked in Germany and across northern Europe at Christmas. Their Dutch cousins, pepernoten, are tossed to children around St. Nicholas Day in the Netherlands.

The flavor comes from a warm mix of spices such as cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, anise and black pepper, often with honey or molasses. Many recipes let the dough or the baked cookies rest for days, which deepens the flavor and softens the texture. A coat of powdered sugar or a thin glaze finishes them.
ways: Bake a batch of pfeffernusse cookies.
Pack cookies in a tin for a friend.
Mix your own warm holiday spice blend.

12-23|Festivus.story:
Festivus reached millions of people through The Strike, a Seinfeld episode that aired in December 1997, written by Dan O'Keefe. He based it on a family holiday his father, Daniel O'Keefe, had invented decades earlier. The TV version added the plain aluminum pole that needs no decorating.

The traditions are meant to be silly: the airing of grievances, where everyone shares how others disappointed them this year, and the feats of strength, where the holiday cannot end until the head of the household is pinned. Many people enjoy it as a lighthearted break from holiday pressure.
ways: Host a friendly airing of grievances.
Stand a broom up as your Festivus pole.
Watch The Strike episode with friends.

12-24|Christmas Eve.story:
Christmas Eve is the evening before Christmas, and for many Christians it is a night for midnight Mass or candlelight services. Families have their own customs, from opening one present early to a big Christmas Eve dinner.

Traditions vary widely. In Italy many families hold a meal of several fish dishes. In Poland the Wigilia supper begins when the first star appears in the sky, and an empty place is often set for an unexpected guest. The carol Silent Night was first performed on Christmas Eve in 1818 in Oberndorf, Austria.
ways: Attend a candlelight service or concert.
Set an extra place for a guest.
Read a Christmas story aloud with family.

12-24|National Eggnog Day.story:
Nobody is sure who first set National Eggnog Day, though Christmas Eve is a natural fit. Eggnog likely descends from posset, a warm drink of milk, wine or ale and spices that was popular in medieval Britain. In the American colonies, it became a rich holiday drink made with eggs, cream, sugar and rum or brandy.

Eggnog even caused a riot. In 1826, cadets at West Point smuggled whiskey in for a Christmas eggnog party, and the night ended in a disturbance now called the Eggnog Riot. For homemade eggnog, cooked custard recipes avoid the safety worries of raw eggs.
ways: Make a cooked custard eggnog at home.
Sprinkle fresh nutmeg on your eggnog.
Bake eggnog flavored cookies or bread.

12-25|Christmas Day.story:
Christians celebrate Christmas as the birth of Jesus. The Bible does not give a date, and the earliest record of December 25 as the celebration comes from Rome in the year 336. Over the centuries the day picked up customs from many places, including evergreen trees from Germany and Santa Claus from Dutch and American traditions.

In the United States, Christmas became a federal holiday in 1870. Today it is celebrated by people of many faiths and none, with church services, family meals, gift giving and quiet time together. Many people also volunteer or reach out to those spending the day alone.
ways: Call someone who is spending today alone.
Share a meal with family or friends.
Take a walk to see the lights.

12-25|National Pumpkin Pie Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Pumpkin Pie Day, but pumpkin pie has a long American story. One of the first American cookbooks, Amelia Simmons's American Cookery from 1796, included a pompkin pudding baked in a crust, which is close to the pie we know.

Pumpkin pie is really a custard. Eggs, milk or cream and pumpkin set together in the oven, flavored with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg and cloves. A common tip is to pull the pie out while the center still jiggles slightly, since it keeps cooking as it cools and cracks if it bakes too long.
ways: Bake a pumpkin pie from scratch.
Make your own pumpkin pie spice blend.
Top a slice with fresh whipped cream.

12-26|Kwanzaa Begins.story:
Kwanzaa runs from December 26 to January 1. Its name comes from the Swahili phrase matunda ya kwanza, meaning first fruits, a nod to harvest festivals across Africa. Each of the seven days honors one principle: unity, self determination, collective work and responsibility, cooperative economics, purpose, creativity and faith.

The main symbol is the kinara, a candleholder with seven candles: one black, three red and three green. A candle is lit each night. Many families also display a mat, ears of corn for the children and a unity cup, and the week ends with a feast called the karamu.
ways: Learn the seven principles with your family.
Support a Black owned local business.
Light a candle and share a family story.

12-26|Boxing Day.story:
Boxing Day falls on December 26, which is also St. Stephen's Day in the Christian calendar. The carol Good King Wenceslas is set on the Feast of Stephen and tells of a king giving to a poor man in the snow, which fits the day's spirit of generosity.

One common explanation is that employers gave servants and tradespeople a Christmas box of money or gifts the day after Christmas, but historians are not certain which story came first. Today in Britain, Canada, Australia and elsewhere it is a public holiday known for sports, leftovers and big sales.
ways: Give a tip or gift to a service worker.
Donate gently used items to charity.
Take a long walk and eat leftovers.

12-27|National Fruitcake Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Fruitcake Day, but cakes packed with dried fruit, nuts and spices have been baked in Europe for centuries, partly because they kept so well through the winter.

Fruitcake keeps because sugar draws water out of the fruit and slows spoilage, and many bakers brush the cake with brandy or rum over several weeks. In Britain a rich fruitcake is the classic Christmas cake and wedding cake, often covered with marzipan and icing. The jokes are mostly an American habit.
ways: Bake a small fruitcake with dried fruits you like.
Try a slice with sharp cheese.
Give fruitcake one fair chance with friends.

12-27|Make a Cut Out Snowflake Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started Make a Cut Out Snowflake Day, but it is a perfect project for the quiet days after Christmas. Folding a paper square into a triangle and cutting shapes along the edges creates a design that repeats as you unfold it.

Real snowflakes have six sides because water molecules lock together in a six sided pattern as they freeze. Wilson Bentley, a farmer in Vermont, was the first person to photograph a single snowflake, in 1885. He took thousands of pictures over his life, which helped popularize the idea that no two look alike.
ways: Fold and cut six sided paper snowflakes.
Hang snowflakes on a window.
Look at Wilson Bentley's snowflake photos.

12-28|National Card Playing Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Card Playing Day, but the days after Christmas are a natural time for games at the kitchen table. Playing cards spread from Asia to Europe by the late 1300s, often carried along trade routes.

The suits most people use today, hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades, come from France in the late 1400s. Simple shapes made the cards cheaper to print with stencils. A single deck can play hundreds of games, from solitaire and rummy to bridge, and many families have house rules passed down for generations.
ways: Teach someone your favorite card game.
Learn a new game like cribbage or euchre.
Play solitaire with a real deck of cards.

12-28|Holy Innocents Day.story:
Holy Innocents Day remembers the children of Bethlehem who, according to the Gospel of Matthew, were killed by order of King Herod as he tried to kill the infant Jesus. In England the day was historically called Childermas. Churches mark it with prayers for children who suffer.

Many Christians today use the day to pray for children affected by war, violence and poverty, and to support groups that protect them. In Spain and much of Latin America it has also become a day for harmless pranks, similar to April Fools' Day, and newspapers sometimes print joke stories.
ways: Pray or reflect on children in need.
Donate to a group that protects children.
Spend focused time with a child you love.

12-29|National Pepper Pot Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Pepper Pot Day. Pepper pot is a thick soup of tripe, vegetables and plenty of black pepper that became famous on the streets of Philadelphia, where vendors sold it hot from kettles.

The popular tale that it was invented at Valley Forge in 1777 is a legend that historians cannot confirm. Food historians point to a deeper root: pepper pot dishes in the Caribbean and West Africa, carried to Philadelphia by enslaved and free Black cooks. Guyana still serves a beloved pepperpot stew at Christmas.
ways: Cook a pot of hearty pepper pot soup.
Try Guyanese pepperpot with bread.
Read about Philadelphia's pepper pot vendors.

12-29|Tick Tock Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started Tick Tock Day, but its message is clear: the year is almost over, so it is a good moment to finish what you can. It falls just a couple of days before New Year's Eve, which leaves enough time for one or two small wins.

The tick tock of a mechanical clock comes from its escapement, a part that releases the gears in tiny regular steps. Each step makes a click. Before that kind of clock, people used sundials, water clocks and candles marked with hours to keep track of time.
ways: Finish one task you have put off.
Clear your email inbox or desk.
Write three goals for next year.

12-30|National Bicarbonate of Soda Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Bicarbonate of Soda Day. Bicarbonate of soda, also called baking soda or sodium bicarbonate, became a kitchen staple in the 1800s, when it helped make quick breads and cakes rise without yeast.

Baking soda needs an acid to work. When it meets buttermilk, yogurt, lemon juice or brown sugar, it releases bubbles of carbon dioxide that lift the batter. Baking powder is baking soda with the acid already mixed in. Around the house, baking soda is used to scrub sinks, absorb fridge odors and freshen drains.
ways: Bake soda bread with buttermilk.
Put an open box of baking soda in the fridge.
Do a baking soda and vinegar volcano with kids.

12-30|National Bacon Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started National Bacon Day. Bacon is pork that has been cured with salt, and often smoked, a way of preserving meat that goes back centuries. American bacon is usually cut from the belly, with streaks of fat, while British back bacon comes from the loin and is leaner.

Canadian bacon in the United States is closer to a lean cured loin, and in Canada it is often called peameal bacon. For crisp bacon, many cooks start it in a cold pan so the fat renders slowly. Baking strips on a tray in the oven also cooks them evenly.
ways: Bake bacon on a sheet pan for even crispness.
Make a classic BLT sandwich.
Try peameal bacon on a breakfast roll.

12-31|New Years Eve.story:
New Year's Eve is the last night of the year in the calendar most of the world uses. People mark it with countdowns, fireworks, songs and wishes. Because of time zones, the first places to greet the new year are islands in the Pacific such as Kiribati, while some American territories are among the last.

The song Auld Lang Syne, sung at midnight in many countries, comes from words Robert Burns wrote down in 1788. In Scotland the night is called Hogmanay. In Spain people eat twelve grapes at midnight, one for each chime of the clock.
ways: Eat twelve grapes at midnight for luck.
Write down three highlights from this year.
Call someone you want to thank.

12-31|Make Up Your Mind Day.story:
Nobody is sure who started Make Up Your Mind Day, but its place on the last day of the year makes sense. It is a nudge to settle the decisions you have been putting off, so you can start the new year with a clear head.

Big choices often feel heavy because every option seems to have a cost. Simple tools can help: write the choice down, list the pros and cons, set a deadline, or ask what you would advise a friend in your place. Sometimes making a good decision now beats waiting for a perfect one.
ways: Make one decision you have been postponing.
Write a pros and cons list for a choice.
Ask a trusted friend for honest advice.

moving|Super Bowl Sunday.story:
The first championship game between the NFL and the AFL was played on January 15, 1967, in Los Angeles, and the Green Bay Packers won. It was not called the Super Bowl at first. The name caught on from Kansas City Chiefs owner Lamar Hunt, who said his children's Super Ball toy gave him the idea.

Today it is one of the most watched broadcasts in the United States each year, with famous ads and a halftime show, and it is one of the biggest eating days of the year, from wings to dips.
ways: Host a watch party where everyone brings a snack.
Run a friendly squares pool for bragging rights only.
Rate the commercials as a family.

moving|Presidents Day.story:
Presidents Day began as Washington's Birthday, celebrated on February 22 and made a holiday for all federal offices in 1885. In 1971 the Uniform Monday Holiday Act moved it to the third Monday in February, which gives workers a long weekend but means it never falls on Washington's actual birthday.

The official federal name is still Washington's Birthday, but many states and stores call it Presidents Day, and many use it to honor Abraham Lincoln too, whose birthday is February 12.
ways: Read a short biography of a president you know little about.
Visit a presidential library, home or memorial.
Quiz your family with presidential trivia.

moving|Leap Day.story:
A year on Earth is about 365 and a quarter days long, so every four years the calendar adds February 29 to stay in step with the seasons. Julius Caesar's calendar added a leap day from 45 BCE, and the Gregorian calendar of 1582 refined the rule: century years skip it unless they divide by 400, which is why 2000 had one and 1900 did not.

In old Irish and British tradition, Leap Day was the one day a woman could propose to a man. People born today, called leaplings, often celebrate on February 28 or March 1 in other years.
ways: Do something you have never done, since today is a bonus day.
Write a letter to yourself to open on the next Leap Day.
Wish a happy birthday to anyone born on February 29.

moving|Daylight Saving Time Begins.story:
In most of the United States, clocks spring forward one hour at 2 a.m. on the second Sunday in March. The idea is to move an hour of daylight from the early morning, when many people are asleep, to the evening.

Benjamin Franklin joked about it in 1784, and the United States first used it in 1918 during World War I. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not change their clocks. The lost hour can leave people groggy for a few days.
ways: Go to bed a little earlier tonight.
Check that every clock, oven and car clock changed.
Swap the batteries in your smoke detectors.

moving|Mardi Gras.story:
Mardi Gras means Fat Tuesday in French. It is the last day before Ash Wednesday and the forty days of Lent, when Christians traditionally fasted, so people feasted and used up rich foods like butter and eggs before it began.

In New Orleans the season brings parades, krewes, beads and king cake with a tiny baby hidden inside, and whoever finds it buys the next cake. The same day is Carnival in Brazil and Venice, and Shrove Tuesday or Pancake Day in Britain.
ways: Bake or buy a king cake and hide the baby.
Make pancakes for Pancake Day.
Dress up in purple, green and gold.

moving|Easter Sunday.story:
Easter is the most important Christian feast, celebrating the resurrection of Jesus. It falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, which puts it between March 22 and April 25.

Many customs are about new life. Eggs were given up during Lent, so they were decorated and eaten on Easter, and German settlers brought the Easter Hare, which became the Easter Bunny, to Pennsylvania in the 1700s. The White House has held an Easter Egg Roll since 1878.
ways: Dye eggs and hold an egg hunt.
Go to a sunrise service or a family brunch.
Bake hot cross buns.

moving|Mothers Day.story:
Anna Jarvis held the first official Mother's Day service in Grafton, West Virginia, in 1908, in memory of her own mother, and handed out white carnations. President Wilson made it a national day in 1914, on the second Sunday in May.

Jarvis insisted on the singular, Mother's Day, one mother honored by one family. She later spent years fighting the greeting card and flower trade over what the day had become.
ways: Write the letter yourself instead of buying the words.
Ask her for a story from before you were born.
Cook, and also do the dishes.

moving|Memorial Day.story:
Memorial Day grew out of Decoration Day after the Civil War, when towns laid flowers on soldiers' graves. General John A. Logan called for a national observance on May 30, 1868, and about 5,000 people decorated graves at Arlington that day.

It moved to the last Monday in May in 1971. The flag flies at half staff until noon and is then raised to the top: grief in the morning, resolve in the afternoon.
ways: Pause at 3 in the afternoon, the National Moment of Remembrance.
Visit a cemetery and read the names.
Place flowers on a grave nobody else has visited.

moving|Fathers Day.story:
Sonora Smart Dodd of Spokane, Washington proposed the day after hearing a Mother's Day sermon. Her father had raised six children alone. Spokane held the first one on June 19, 1910.

It took decades to catch on. President Nixon signed it into law in 1972, on the third Sunday in June.
ways: Ask him to teach you the one thing he is best at.
Look through old photos and write the dates on the back.
Let him pick the music.

moving|Labor Day.story:
Unions in New York held the first Labor Day parade on September 5, 1882, when a working day of ten or twelve hours was common. Congress made it a national holiday in 1894, weeks after the deadly Pullman railroad strike.

Two men with nearly the same name, Matthew Maguire and Peter McGuire, have both been credited with the idea, and historians still argue over it.
ways: Thank someone who works the holiday shift.
Read about the trade a grandparent worked in.
Take the whole day off, if you can.

moving|National Grandparents Day.story:
Marian McQuade of West Virginia campaigned for the day, hoping children would visit and learn from older people. President Carter signed the proclamation in 1978, and it falls on the first Sunday after Labor Day.

The date was chosen for the autumn years of life. Its official flower is the forget me not.
ways: Record a short interview on your phone.
Ask for the recipe nobody wrote down.
Visit an older neighbor who has no family nearby.

moving|Daylight Saving Time Ends.story:
On the first Sunday in November most of the United States sets clocks back one hour at 2 in the morning. Germany was the first country to adopt the change nationwide, in 1916, to save fuel during the war.

Hawaii and most of Arizona skip it. Getting the hour back is easier on sleep than losing it in spring, but evening darkness arrives abruptly.
ways: Change smoke alarm batteries while you change the clocks.
Get outside in the morning light for a few days.
Check bike and car lights before the first dark commute.

moving|Thanksgiving.story:
In the fall of 1621, the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony and about 90 Wampanoag men led by Massasoit shared a harvest feast that lasted three days. It was not called Thanksgiving at the time, and the menu likely had venison and wild fowl rather than the dinner we know now.

Days of thanks came and went for two centuries, until the writer Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for a national holiday. President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed one in 1863, and a 1941 law fixed it on the fourth Thursday of November. For many Native Americans it is also a day of remembrance.
ways: Go around the table and share one thing you are thankful for.
Invite someone who would otherwise spend the day alone.
Take a walk together between dinner and dessert.

moving|Black Friday.story:
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, and for decades it has marked the start of the holiday shopping season in the United States. Philadelphia police used the name in the 1950s and 1960s for the crowds and traffic that jammed the city that day.

A later explanation says it is the day stores move from red ink to black and turn a profit, a story retailers liked better. Today the deals start earlier and run online all weekend.
ways: Make a list and a budget before you shop.
Shop at a local small business instead of a big chain.
Skip the stores and take a walk or watch a movie.

moving|Giving Tuesday.story:
Giving Tuesday began in 2012 as a project of the 92nd Street Y in New York and the United Nations Foundation. After Black Friday and Cyber Monday, it offered a different kind of day, one for giving back.

It has grown into a movement around the world. Gifts of money matter, but so do time, skills and kindness, from volunteering to donating blood to checking on a neighbor.
ways: Give to a cause you care about, any amount.
Sign up for a volunteer shift this month.
Donate blood or help set up a blood drive.

moving|National Fruitcake Toss Day.story:
National Fruitcake Toss Day comes after the holidays, when leftover fruitcakes are looking for a new purpose. The best known toss is the Great Fruitcake Toss in Manitou Springs, Colorado, which began in 1996 and sends fruitcakes flying by hand, slingshot and homemade launcher.

Fruitcake has a long history, from Roman cakes made with pomegranate seeds and pine nuts to the dense, boozy loaves of Victorian England, which keep for months.
ways: Hold a backyard fruitcake toss and measure the distance.
Give fruitcake a fair chance with a fresh slice.
Turn a leftover one into trifle or bread pudding.

moving|Martin Luther King Jr. Day.story:
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was born on January 15, 1929, in Atlanta. A Baptist minister, he led the Montgomery bus boycott, helped organize the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave his I Have a Dream speech, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

President Ronald Reagan signed the holiday into law in 1983, and it was first observed in 1986 on the third Monday in January. In 1994 Congress made it a national day of service: a day on, not a day off.
ways: Volunteer for a service project in your community.
Read or listen to the I Have a Dream speech in full.
Visit a civil rights museum or memorial.

moving|National Donut Day.story:
The Salvation Army held the first one in Chicago in 1938 to honor its Donut Lassies, volunteers who fried donuts for soldiers near the front in France during the First World War, sometimes in a helmet. It falls on the first Friday in June.

There are two main families: yeast donuts, risen and airy, and cake donuts, raised with baking powder and crumbly at the edge.
ways: Go early; the best ones are gone by nine.
Fry one batch at home at a steady 350 to 375 degrees.
Bring a box to a fire station.

moving|World Smile Day.story:
Harvey Ball, a commercial artist in Worcester, Massachusetts, drew the yellow smiley face in 1963 to lift morale at an insurance company. It took about ten minutes, he was paid $45, and he never trademarked it.

Worried that the symbol had become only a product, he started World Smile Day in 1999, on the first Friday in October, with the request to do one kind act.
ways: Do one kind thing and tell nobody.
Send a photo that made you laugh.
Compliment a stranger on something they chose.

moving|National Ugly Sweater Day.story:
National Ugly Sweater Day falls on the third Friday of December and celebrates the gloriously tacky holiday sweater. Bulky Christmas knits with reindeer and snowflakes were popular in the 1980s, faded, then came back as a joke in the early 2000s when friends began throwing ugly sweater parties.

Now the sweaters are loud on purpose, with tinsel, bells and blinking lights. Many schools and offices use the day to raise money, like Save the Children's Christmas Jumper Day in the UK.
ways: Wear your loudest holiday sweater all day.
Host an ugly sweater contest with silly prizes.
Decorate a plain sweater with felt, pom poms and bells.
